summary: A humorous, satirical incident-report-style essay dated September 8, 2023 about a widespread internet outage and its effect on consumers. It portrays panic, a return to analog life, and frustration with customer service and Service Level Agreements (SLAs) that promise 99.9% uptime but yield only token compensation. It ends with calls from consumer advocates for stricter SLAs and fair compensation for outages.
one_line: Satirical account of an internet outage, weak SLA compensation, and consumer activists demanding stronger service guarantees and fair recompense.
key_facts: The note is dated September 8, 2023 and is categorized as an Incident Report, though written in a whimsical, satirical tone.
Mrs. Felicity Goodbutton of Pleasantville wakes to find her smart coffee maker has stopped working during the outage.
Janet McNotaninfluencer, described as a lip-sync legend and consumer rights advocate, reads from an SLA: "..shall endeavor to provide 99.9% network uptime…"
On September 12th, Adrian Quibble asked for a week's credit for an 8-hour outage.
Adrian Quibble's reply from the provider was a coupon for three free emoticons, one of which wasn't even smiling.
Customer service representatives respond with scripted empathy and phrases like "I understand your frustration" followed by "Unfortunately, we cannot…"
Bryan Wistful, a rediscovered dog owner, says "I didn't even know I had a puppy" after being offline.
Some people used the outage to read books, meditate and grow gardens, treating it as a reset on digital addiction.
Consumer Crusaders call for stricter SLAs, transparency, and compensation beyond emoticon pacifiers.
A second outage occurred on September 20th, which the note suggests may have been an echo of the first.
Linda Byte, a small business owner turned activist, says "We need guarantees, not just pacifiers!"
Linda Byte founded a union called 'Disconnection Discontents' that rallies for equitable recompense for outages.
